subject_matter.value: Freshman Melinda, shunned for calling police to a summer party, recalls being raped there by senior Andy Evans and finally names what happened.

literary_form.evidence: A play monologue spoken under the label SPOONFACE with page markers and directions such as "(makes a serious face)".

tone.evidence: A dying child speaks with wonder about "magic sparks" and finding meaning while alive.

content_warnings.evidence: She retells the Holocaust: a soldier "hit her Mam on the head and shot her and then she died", and children were "going to get gassed".

difficulty.evidence: A sustained childlike, non-standard voice ("I can't speak proper") carrying a wide range from comedy to death.

performance_demands.evidence: Written regional child speech such as "Mam came running" and "the sparks what would save me".

audience_level.evidence: Terminal illness and Holocaust killings are described through a child's eyes without extended graphic detail.

themes.evidence: "So this is all because I am autistic" and "the whole point of living is to find the spark".

subject_matter.value: Spoonface, an autistic girl dying of cancer, describes her gift for numbers, her diagnosis, a doctor's Holocaust stories and her belief that sparks will carry her to heaven.
subject_matter.evidence: "The doctor said that I was going to die" and "the sparks would fly up and take me to heaven".

literary_form.evidence: A monologue from the play Commencement with speaker labels SARAH and MITCHELL.

tone.evidence: A shooter's mother waits alone and pieces together "this jigsaw puzzle of my son".

content_warnings.evidence: Her son killed classmates ("spent the last moments of their lives"), was beaten ("Black eyes that looked like black holes") and shot himself ("slipped the gun over his tongue").

difficulty.evidence: Calm, observant narration builds to a graphic revelation, with brief scenes voicing a withdrawn son.

performance_demands.evidence: Repeated exchanges where Mitchell answers "I don’t want to talk about it" punctuate a slowly building monologue.

audience_level.evidence: A school shooting and a graphic suicide are described.

themes.evidence: "no one will weep for mine" and "I never saw tragedy coming".

subject_matter.value: Hidden in a hospital pediatric waiting room after her son's school shooting, Sarah recalls his childhood injuries and bullying before revealing he killed himself.
subject_matter.evidence: "They gave me my own waiting room" and "When Mitchell was done, he slipped the gun".

literary_form.evidence: A play with speaker labels M’LYNN, SHELBY and ANNELLE and directions such as "(Pause)".

tone.evidence: Shelby's joy over a baby ("thirty minutes of wonderful") gives way to M’Lynn's grief at her death.

content_warnings.evidence: M’Lynn describes Shelby's death ("They turned off the machines") and rages in grief ("I'm so mad I don't know what to do!!").

difficulty.evidence: Three characters, echoed memory lines, and a climax that moves from calm to "sobbing/screaming".

performance_demands.evidence: Shelby's lines return as "(echoes)" between M’Lynn's breakdown, including "I'm FINE! [sobbing/screaming]".

audience_level.evidence: A daughter's death from illness and a mother's grief with no graphic content.

themes.evidence: "I would rather have thirty minutes of wonderful" and "I wanna know WHY".

subject_matter.value: Diabetic Shelby tells her mother she is pregnant despite the risk, later needs her mother's kidney, and after Shelby dies M'Lynn breaks down while remembering her words.
subject_matter.evidence: "I'm pregnant." and "Mama’s going to give me one of her kidneys."

literary_form.evidence: A monologue-driven script with speaker labels SUSAN, RICKY, AUNT, FATHER and GINA and a written "(Beat; to audience)".

tone.evidence: "The Summer of '95. It was the best time for me" turns to "Ricky was dead. Dead. Dead."

content_warnings.evidence: Racist remarks ("Didn't know you liked dark meat", "everyone ought to own one"), Ricky's death in a car that "had been tampered with", and her grief and miscarriage.

difficulty.evidence: A narrator with several brief character voices, moving from wry humor to shock and grief.

performance_demands.evidence: Brief lines from the woman, aunt and father, and the timed countdown "8:00: Ricky hadn't returned. 8:30: nothing."

audience_level.evidence: Racism, a death and a miscarriage are described without graphic detail.

themes.evidence: "Race did matter" and "Moments forever remembered in black and white."

subject_matter.value: Susan recalls her 1995 romance with Ricky, a Black man, amid racist disapproval, and his death in her sabotaged car shortly before she lost their baby.
subject_matter.evidence: "Ricky and I met at the Wash-n-Save Laundromat" and "he was driving my car".

literary_form.evidence: A first-person testimony monologue from a documentary theatre collection, spoken under the label FATMEH with page markers.

tone.evidence: The closing plea "Stop the war, the destruction and the killing."

content_warnings.evidence: She describes army and rebel checkpoints, "the army’s boots and bombs" and fleeing at night with smugglers.

difficulty.evidence: One narrator who quotes her son, soldiers and smugglers and builds to an impassioned refrain.

performance_demands.evidence: The repeated refrain "Stop the war." and quoted shouts such as "Stop the babies from crying".

audience_level.evidence: War and flight are described without graphic violence.

themes.evidence: "I miss my country, my home" and "You have promised your child."

subject_matter.value: A Syrian mother recalls her son charming soldiers at checkpoints, then fleeing pregnant with him across hills to Jordan, and pleads with world leaders to stop the war.
subject_matter.evidence: "Taher, my little boy, used to distinguish between checkpoints" and "towards the Jordanian border".

literary_form.evidence: A monologue from a published collection of plays, spoken under the label MOLLY.

tone.evidence: Molly plans to kill the car company president and then say "WOOPS. So sorry."

content_warnings.evidence: The car kept "ramming itself into my child" who "later died in the hospital", her husband "began to drink", and she plans to drive a man "into the wall".

difficulty.evidence: One voice that moves from calm recollection through horror to cold resolve.

audience_level.evidence: A child's violent death and a planned killing are described.

themes.evidence: "The big boys take care of each other" and "It was my fault."

subject_matter.value: After her new car suddenly accelerates and kills her son and a commission blames her, a ruined mother calmly describes her plan to run down the car company's president.
subject_matter.evidence: "the car lurched forward violently into my little boy" and "I will step on the gas".

literary_form.evidence: A play monologue with stage directions such as "sets up a video camera on a tripod" and the label SUSAN.

tone.evidence: A child-killer auditions for talk shows and says "Sometimes I think I am the bravest woman I know."

content_warnings.evidence: Susan admits "I wanted to commit suicide" and describes drowning her sons ("I had to end our lives").

difficulty.evidence: Sustained Southern dialect and a self-deluding voice that shifts across three tapes to a chilling confession.

performance_demands.evidence: Written dialect ("Those boys was always clean") and business such as "She stops the camera, rewinds".

audience_level.evidence: A mother's killing of her children and her suicidal intent are described.

themes.evidence: "I need to have my time to make my say" and "Evil things happened to me."

subject_matter.value: From prison, Susan Smith records audition tapes for Oprah, Jerry Springer and Barbara Walters, justifying and finally recounting how she drowned her two young sons.
subject_matter.evidence: "Miss Oprah, I hope you still remember me" and "I wanted to see the lake".

literary_form.evidence: A monologue play from a collection of monologue plays, written in lineated free verse ("My name is Tamam. It means enough.").

tone.evidence: Tamam recounts rape in a jail and her brother's bombing, insisting "no one is going to reduce me to a coin."

content_warnings.evidence: Guards "raped me in front of him" and beat her brother, he "blew up that bus" killing passengers, the occupiers "refer to us as the cockroaches", and her husband "calls me a whore".

difficulty.evidence: A long verse monologue moving among irony, horror, love, rage and political argument, with the brother's quoted speech.

performance_demands.evidence: Lineated verse and refrains such as "It's not a boast. It's a fact." and the closing return to "It means enough."

audience_level.evidence: Rape used as torture and a suicide bombing are described.

themes.evidence: "I am the kind of human being who refuses to get high on the drug of hate" and "none of them love you like I do, brother."

subject_matter.value: Tamam, a young woman from Gaza, tells how Israeli guards raped her in front of her jailed brother, how he later became a suicide bomber, and how her fiance abandoned her.
subject_matter.evidence: "I went to the jail to visit my brother" and "My love left me".

literary_form.evidence: A first-person memoir passage in paragraphs ("I was ten the first time I stepped on a scale") with no speaker labels.

tone.evidence: Wry humor ("But it's a big state") sits with pain over "I love you, but you're fat."

content_warnings.evidence: Her eating becomes "the early seeds of an addiction" and her sister shows signs of anorexia ("my sister was still wasting away").

difficulty.evidence: One narrator who voices her grandmother and mother, shifting from humor to hurt to adult reflection.

performance_demands.evidence: Quoted voices such as Grandma's "Girls have to be thin and beautiful" and her mother's "Where the h ell did this go?".

audience_level.evidence: Body shaming and disordered eating are described without graphic content.

themes.evidence: "the world judges on first appearances" and "most people are simply doing the best they can".

subject_matter.value: Journalist Abby Ellin recalls her grandmother's and mother's efforts to make her thin, hiding food as a teen while her sister starved herself, and her later understanding of her parents.
subject_matter.evidence: "You need to lose fifteen pounds" and "My sister and I both received the same messages about fat".

literary_form.evidence: A play with speaker labels CATHERINE, TOM, MR. REED and DR. DALITSCH, page markers and scene directions.

tone.evidence: A proud first workday ("Do I look like a girl worth 8 cents a watch?") ends with her death and "time stood still for just a minute"

content_warnings.evidence: Catherine is poisoned by radium, "She died 21 days later", and Tom grieves ("what I’m going to do with all this goddamn time?").

difficulty.evidence: Several characters, overlapping time frames and a physical decline from vitality to dying.

performance_demands.evidence: Directions such as "we see her physically deteriorate in pain" and repeated "(Long pause)" over a ticking watch.

audience_level.evidence: Illness and death are described without graphic violence.

themes.evidence: "It’s a crime!" and "Women like me don’t stir up trouble."

subject_matter.value: Catherine Donohue takes a dial-painting job at Radium Dial, is poisoned by the radium paint, is fired and sues the company before dying, while her husband Tom grieves.
subject_matter.evidence: "this is a direct result of radium poisoning" and "Our case went to court."

literary_form.evidence: A play with opening stage direction "Lights up on Mac" and speaker labels MAC, GRANDMA, DAD and MORTON.

tone.evidence: Wisecracks about corpse-robbing ("Grandma'll be a cinch") give way to the revelation that her family died.

content_warnings.evidence: Mac says "I tried to kill myself" in the garage, and the fumes "had killed my family" while she slept; her grandmother lies in the casket.

difficulty.evidence: Seven characters, a time-jumping structure ("Let me go back.") and a range from comedy to devastation.

performance_demands.evidence: The refrain "Let me go back." and business such as "Mac kneels and begins to remove her rings".

audience_level.evidence: A suicide attempt that killed the speaker's family is described.

themes.evidence: "Why can't you love the littlest things?" and "It is not what I want or need."

subject_matter.value: Mac, who steals jewelry from corpses, returns home to take her grandmother's ring from the casket and reveals that her suicide attempt killed her husband and children.
subject_matter.evidence: "I've been stealing jewelry off corpses for years" and "it had killed my family".

literary_form.evidence: A short story from a story collection, delivered as a first-person monologue under the added label RACHEL.

tone.evidence: Rachel jokes ("who asks for a refund for a seven-dollar high school play?") about a classmate's death.

content_warnings.evidence: She recounts that "Scotty King got electrocuted while running the light board" and "he died".

difficulty.evidence: One voice that swings between nervous humor, guilt and determination.

audience_level.evidence: An accidental death is recounted without graphic detail.

themes.evidence: "you’ve had trouble remembering my name" and "The show must go on."

subject_matter.value: At an audition, Rachel performs a monologue she wrote about being overlooked, about the stage crew death of Scotty who replaced her on the light board, and about wanting a part at last.
subject_matter.evidence: "I wrote it." and "it was supposed to be me".
